Six Elements, One Comparison

A teaching companion to Quotients, Refinement and Reconstruction

Henry Shin · October 2026

This is a concrete first route into Quotients, Refinement, and Reconstruction. Links marked main § lead to its general arguments and higher chapters.

Ways through this companion

First pass: read §§1–8 in order, following the same six elements through the constructions. Pause at each check before continuing.

Try the maps: work through the seven exercises (§10), then compare the worked answers (§11).

Continue when ready: §9 computes the optional spectral comparison; §12 gives prerequisites and starting points for the higher chapters.

The general argument: return to main §§1–4.5 for the exact Mal’cev framework, Jordan–Hölder, and invariance of dimension.

This booklet starts with addition modulo six and follows one example through the comparison argument behind Jordan–Hölder. You need subgroups and cosets; the categorical language is introduced only after its job becomes visible. Read §§1–8 as the main route. Section 9 is an optional spectral calculation, §§10–11 contain exercises and answers, and §12 is a guide to the higher chapters. References marked main § lead to the full exposition.

5 · Why the construction works beyond six elements

Let be any subgroup relation. Restrict to its input and output supports , . Set and . They are reflexive on these supports and symmetric by definition.

For transitivity of , suppose share output , and share output . The three corners give , so share . Interchanging input and output proves transitivity of . Thus are equivalence relations on their supports.

They respect the group operations. For example, witnesses for and give witness for ; inversion of a witness gives the corresponding inverse relation. The same holds for . Their classes therefore carry well-defined quotient group structures.

Define

An output exists by the definition of support. Different outputs for the same are -related. If , choose a common output ; any outputs for and are each -related to . Hence the formula is independent of both choices. Reversing constructs its inverse. Finally, and imply , so is a homomorphism.

This proof is the small mechanism inside the comparison theorem:

The abstract framework packages precisely the operations just used:

StructureWork it performs
Finite limitsForm pairs satisfying equations and the spaces of witnesses.
Regular imagesForm supports and compose relations.
Barr exactnessMake equivalence relations into effective quotients.
Mal'cev propertySupply the three-corner property for internal relations.
PointednessSupply a zero object and zero classes for the later series argument.

Pointedness is needed for that formulation of normal series, not for the common-quotient construction itself. Groups and modules provide these structures; the full exposition establishes the categorical relation calculus before using it.

Pause and check. The conclusion is an isomorphism characterized by a commuting diagram, not merely equality of the numbers of classes.

This page proves the group mechanism. The proof for every exact Mal'cev category, with its image and quotient dependencies, is in main §1 and main §2.

8 · Why simplicity turns comparison into a matching

Read the rectangle rowwise to get ; read it columnwise to get . Delete the trivial factors. The matching is given by actual maps:

No equality of lengths was needed to build these maps.

Here is the general final step for groups. A finite normal series in a nontrivial simple group has exactly one nontrivial factor. Look at the first term equal to . Its preceding term is a proper normal subgroup of , hence is trivial. Every earlier term is therefore trivial, and every later term is . Notice that this argument needs only normality in the next term.

The general refinement theorem, proved in main §3, constructs a rectangle of paired factors for two finite normal series. If the original series are composition series, each row is a refinement of a simple quotient, so exactly one nontrivial cell survives in that row. The same holds in each column. Those surviving cells give a bijection between the original factors, with an isomorphism for each matched pair. Equality of the numbers of factors is a consequence of this bijection.

This booklet has computed that construction for and proved its common-quotient mechanism for groups. The full categorical refinement theorem is supplied by the main exposition; a successful six-element calculation is not a substitute for that theorem.

Dimension now follows. For a finite basis of a vector space over , put . The map

is onto by the definition of span and injective by linear independence. The -module is simple: a submodule containing a nonzero contains , hence every scalar. A second finite basis therefore gives another composition series, and Jordan–Hölder gives the same number of steps. For , every basis is empty, directly by independence.

What this example does not test. is abelian, and the map , , is an isomorphism by §1. Thus all our subgroups are ambient-normal and this extension splits. Exercise 6 tests adjacent normality in . Exercise 7 shows that the same simple factors can assemble into different groups.

Pause and check. This is a complete stopping point for the teaching route. The higher chapters ask what the list of factors forgets, and what extra structure can retain or recover that information.

12 · A guide to the higher chapters

The comparison theorem is already complete before the higher chapters. Those chapters pursue a new question: what additional structure is retained by richer quotients and more informative probes? The following routes use the main exposition's section numbers.

First bridge: stay with ordinary algebra. Main §9 studies attachment data and marked extensions: besides the two end objects, retain how one sits inside the total object and how the total object maps onto the other. It also explains why data from adjacent layers can miss information across a skipped layer. Main §10 studies probes for nilpotent operators and reconstructs their chains. Modules and linear algebra suffice for this route. Exercise 7 gives the simplest reason to want it: a factor list does not determine the assembled object.

First higher bridge: an orbit can hide a stabilizer. Start with main §12.2. A groupoid is a category in which every arrow is invertible. For a group action, its action groupoid has the acted-on points as objects and the group elements carrying one point to another as arrows.

Let act by addition on the two-element set . The action is transitive, so its ordinary orbit set is a single point. But the stabilizer of either point is . The action groupoid retains these automorphisms. Its full subgroupoid on the object has one object and automorphism group ; it is equivalent to the whole groupoid because every other object is isomorphic to . Writing for the classifying space of a group , we get

The double slash denotes the homotopy quotient, obtained by realizing the action groupoid. It remembers something the orbit set discarded.

Next bridge: intersections acquire components and loops. Read main §12.3 for the homotopy-pullback construction. The double-coset formula proved in main §12.6 gives, for subgroups ,

Here the superscript denotes a homotopy pullback. In our abelian example, and , so

With on both sides there are three double cosets and each intersection is , giving

An ordinary subgroup intersection sees the group in the identity component. The homotopy pullback records the other components too.

Pause and check. At each stage ask which object is being used. The orbit set forgets stabilizers; the action groupoid and its classifying homotopy -type retain equivalent information.

Choose a route by the question you want to answer. The higher chapters need not be read in numerical order.

Main sectionsPreparationQuestion and payoff
§12.1, §§12.4–5, §12.7Spaces, homotopy pullbacks and universal propertiesHow do coherent algebraic models, base change and descent organize quotients? What extra structure replaces ordinary normality?
§§13.1–2Groups, semidirect products and modulesWhat does linearization retain when performed over a fixed group? The base retains the group action on coefficients.
§13.3Spectra, truncations and descentHow do spectra over extend these coefficients across degrees? The heart recovers ordinary -modules.
§§13.4–5Complexes, cohomology, projective resolutions and derived categoriesHow are marked extensions and their automorphisms recorded? Why can derived tensor products have additional homology?
§13.6Derivations and commutative algebra, followed by cotangent complexesHow does cotangent transitivity identify the obstruction to extending a derivation?

For an algebraic entry to this table, read §13.1 and §13.2 before attempting spectra. An abelian group object over is equivalent to a -module:

The zero section splits the map to ; its kernel is abelian, and conjugation by that section gives the -action. Conversely a -module produces its semidirect product over . Thus linearizing over a base retains more than forgetting the base and taking an ordinary abelian group.

Three questions keep the higher route precise. First, what is the ambient category? A descent result for an -topos does not automatically hold in every category of algebraic models. Second, what extra data are retained—a base, marked endpoints, automorphisms, or coherent homotopies? Third, what is actually concluded? An obstruction group names possible obstructions; a particular lifting problem has a particular obstruction class whose vanishing must be checked.

The main exposition identifies the higher foundations it imports. These chapters enrich quotient and reconstruction questions; they do not claim a Jordan–Hölder theorem for arbitrary higher objects. The ordinary refinement proof does not depend on them.
